text: The product-form derivation from last lesson showed that the QFT output factors into a tensor product of single-qubit states. This lesson turns that algebraic fact into an actual sequence of gates — the circuit a real quantum computer runs.

The building block is the controlled phase rotation gate, R sub k, which leaves ket zero alone and multiplies ket one by a phase — R sub 1 is just the Z gate. A controlled-R-k gate applies that rotation to a target qubit only when a control qubit is one, the standard controlled-gate pattern. Each bit of the input contributes exactly one controlled rotation into the phase each output qubit needs to carry. And because the main construction naturally produces qubits in bit-reversed order, a final swap network is needed at the end to undo that reversal.

Here's the complete gate sequence for 3 qubits. Hadamard on q1, then controlled-R2 from q2 and controlled-R3 from q3 onto q1. Hadamard on q2, then controlled-R2 from q3 onto q2. Hadamard on q3. And finally swap q1 with q3. That's 7 gates total — 3 Hadamards, 3 controlled-phase gates, and 1 swap — to transform a full 8-dimensional amplitude vector.

Counting across all n qubits: n Hadamards, one per qubit. N times n-minus-1 over 2 controlled-phase gates, since qubit 1 gets n-minus-1 rotations, qubit 2 gets n-minus-2, down to qubit n getting zero. And up to floor of n over 2 swaps to reverse the full qubit order. Add it up and the total is O of n squared gates — a count of gates on qubits, not arithmetic operations on classical numbers. Next lesson is exactly about what that comparison does and doesn't tell you.

Next lesson is the honesty check: the QFT circuit really is exponentially cheaper gate-for-gate than the classical FFT — but that comparison hides a catch that makes or breaks every algorithm built on top of it.
